entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8344"/><div sID="gen13314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8344"/><hi type="bold">7. gold--</hi>forbidden to be heaped together (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.17">De 17:17</reference>). Solomon disobeyed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">1Ki 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses ... chariots--</hi>forbidden (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>). But Solomon disobeyed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">1Ki 20:26</reference>). Horses could be used effectively for war in the plains of Egypt; not so in the hilly Judea. God designed there should be as wide as possible a distinction between Israel and the Egyptians. He would have His people wholly dependent on Him, rather than on the ordinary means of warfare (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>). Also horses were connected with idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>); hence His objection: so the transition to "idols" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Is 2:8</reference>) is natural. <div eID="gen13315" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8353"/><div sID="gen13332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8353"/><hi type="bold">16. Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus in southwest Spain, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, near Gibraltar. It includes the adjoining region: a Phoenician colony; hence its connection with Palestine and the Bible (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.21">2Ch 9:21</reference>). The name was also used in a wide sense for the farthest west, as our West Indies (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">72:10</reference>). "Ships of Tarshish" became a phrase for richly laden and far-voyaging vessels. The judgment shall be on all that minister to man's luxury (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.18.17-Rev.18.19">Re 18:17-19</reference>).<div eID="gen13332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pictures--</hi>ordered to be destroyed (<reference osisRef="Num.33.52">Nu 33:52</reference>). Still to be seen on the walls of Nineveh's palaces. It is remarkable that whereas all other ancient civilized nations, Egypt, Assyria, Greece, Rome, have left monuments in the fine arts, Judea, while rising immeasurably above them in the possession of "the living oracles," has left none of the former. The fine arts, as in modern Rome, were so often associated with polytheism, that God required His people in this, as in other respects, to be separate from the nations (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.15-Deut.4.18">De 4:15-18</reference>). But Vulgate translation is perhaps better, "All that is beautiful to the sight"; not only paintings, but all luxurious ornaments. One comprehensive word for all that goes before (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12">Re 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.16">14, 16</reference>). <div eID="gen13333" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 16. Tarshish-- Tartessus in southwest Spain, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, near Gibraltar. It includes the adjoining region: a Phoenician colony; hence its connection with Palestine and the Bible ( 2Ch 9:21 ). The name was also used in a wide sense for the farthest west, as our West Indies ( Is 66:19 ; Psa 48:7 ; 72:10 ). "Ships of Tarshish" became a phrase for richly laden and far-voyaging vessels. The judgment shall be on all that minister to man's luxury (compare Re 18:17-19 ). pictures-- ordered to be destroyed ( Nu 33:52 ). Still to be seen on the walls of Nineveh's palaces. It is remarkable that whereas all other ancient civilized nations, Egypt, Assyria, Greece, Rome, have left monuments in the fine arts, Judea, while rising immeasurably above them in the possession of "the living oracles," has left none of the former. The fine arts, as in modern Rome, were so often associated with polytheism, that God required His people in this, as in other respects, to be separate from the nations ( De 4:15-18 ). But Vulgate translation is perhaps better, "All that is beautiful to the sight"; not only paintings, but all luxurious ornaments. One comprehensive word for all that goes before (compare Re 18:12 , 14, 16 ).
entries.reader_content_plain: 16. Tarshish-- Tartessus in southwest Spain, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, near Gibraltar. It includes the adjoining region: a Phoenician colony; hence its connection with Palestine and the Bible ( 2Ch 9:21 ). The name was also used in a wide sense for the farthest west, as our West Indies ( Is 66:19 ; Psa 48:7 ; 72:10 ). "Ships of Tarshish" became a phrase for richly laden and far-voyaging vessels. The judgment shall be on all that minister to man's luxury (compare Re 18:17-19 ). pictures-- ordered to be destroyed ( Nu 33:52 ). Still to be seen on the walls of Nineveh's palaces. It is remarkable that whereas all other ancient civilized nations, Egypt, Assyria, Greece, Rome, have left monuments in the fine arts, Judea, while rising immeasurably above them in the possession of "the living oracles," has left none of the former. The fine arts, as in modern Rome, were so often associated with polytheism, that God required His people in this, as in other respects, to be separate from the nations ( De 4:15-18 ). But Vulgate translation is perhaps better, "All that is beautiful to the sight"; not only paintings, but all luxurious ornaments. One comprehensive word for all that goes before (compare Re 18:12 , 14, 16 ).
